Learning Objectives
Review the definition and clinical classification of concussion.
Assess and treat patients with concussions in the subacute outpatient setting.
Apply clearance and return-to-play guidelines for concussion.
Compare the differential diagnosis and treatment options for persistent post-concussive
symptoms.

A concussion is a trauma-induced transient alteration in neurologic function that may or may
not involve loss of consciousness.1
Concussion is a subset of mild traumatic brain injury, which is defined by a Glasgow Coma
Scale score ranging from 13 to 15. Concussion is a term typically used in the context of sport.1
Epidemiology
Between 2 and 4 million sport-related traumatic brain injuries occur in the United States each
year, most of which are diagnosed as concussion.2
Approximately 10% of people in the United States will experience a concussion.3
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Concussion is caused by a sudden impact to the head, or elsewhere on the body, with forces
transmitted to the head that cause disturbance in brain physiology.
A common mechanism of injury is sudden deceleration of the head.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Concussion is caused by a sudden impact to the head, or elsewhere on the body, with
forces transmitted to the head that cause stretching of neuronal axons and increases in
ionic permeability.1 Cellular transport channels are activated to maintain homeostasis,
which depletes energy stores, leading to a global hypometabolic state. In animal models,
this phase lasts 7 to 10 days, during which the brain is particularly vulnerable to
repeated trauma and physiologic stressors (ie, excessive cognitive or physical activity,
sleep deprivation).4
Risk Factors
Combat/contact sports, such as wrestling, football, and ice hockey, are associated with a
higher risk of concussion; however, concussions can occur in any sport.
Neck muscle weakness is a potential risk factor for concussion.

Adolescent age group
Type of force applied to the head/brain (rotational being worse than linear)

Risk Factors
The mean recovery time for adults and children (younger than 12 years) with concussion
typically is less than 2 weeks; however, the mean recovery time for adolescents typically
is longer, lasting as many as 4 weeks.5,6 The exact reason for this difference is unknown
but is suspected to be because of increased brain and limb-length development during
puberty and increased vulnerability.7 Female sex is a risk factor for a concussion;
however, the exact cause of this is unknown and may be because of physical size
differences and neck girth.8 Historically, female sex also has been associated with
prolonged recovery from a concussion; however, recent prospective studies suggest no
difference in recovery time if males and females are treated in a similar manner.9,10
Associated Injuries
At the time of injury, patients should be evaluated for more serious injuries, such as
intracranial bleeding or cervical spine injury.
Transport to a hospital should be considered for patients who demonstrate the following:
Persistent drowsiness or declining level of consciousness
Spinal cord symptoms
Loss of consciousness exceeding 1 minute
Seizure (and possibly tonic posturing) in a patient with no history of seizure
Deep scalp laceration with substantial blood loss
Worsening headache, especially if accompanied by recurrent vomiting
Severe neck pain
Difficulty moving the arms or legs
Any lateralizing neurologic sign, such as motor asymmetry, pupil asymmetry, or hemisensory
loss
Injury Classification

The primary goal of the first outpatient visit, which usually occurs 48 hours or more postinjury,
is to confirm the diagnosis of concussion, identify impairments on a pertinent physical
examination, and create an individualized treatment plan.
Concussion is a clinical diagnosis. No preferred biomarker is available to diagnose concussion.
Acute concussion is defined as occurring within hours to days of the head injury while
symptoms are still evolving. Subacute concussion is defined as occurring within days to a few
weeks of the head injury, and patients typically are seen at outpatient clinics. Persistent post-
concussive symptoms (PPCS) is the term used to describe symptoms that linger for more than
2 weeks in adults and more than 1 month in adolescents.1
 Concussion and PPCS can be classified into the following clinical profiles, which may overlap:
physiologic/autonomic, vestibulo-ocular, cervical, and mood/cognition3 (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Algorithm shows the classification and management of concussion and persistent post-
concussive symptoms. (Courtesy of M. Nadir Haider, MD, Buffalo, NY.)


Injury Classification
Acute concussions typically are identified on the sideline, in the emergency department,
or by a school nurse. Symptoms attributable to concussion should emerge within 24 to
48 hours of injury. New symptoms reported to occur more than 24 to 48 hours
postinjury may be related to other conditions or injuries. Orthopaedic surgeons, even
those who have completed a sports medicine fellowship, are not expected to treat
athletes with a concussion on the sideline or replace neurologists/neuropsychologists in
long-term management; however, they should understand the pathophysiology of
concussion so they can work in concert with and assist sports medicine physicians,
athletic trainers, and physical therapists to provide comprehensive care to athletes with
a concussion.11
Physiologic/autonomic concussion is thought to result from a global cerebral metabolic
disturbance that involves autonomic nervous system dysfunction and abnormal cerebral
blood flow regulation, especially during exercise.12 It is associated with early symptom-
limited exercise intolerance (ie, exercise limited by concussion-like symptom
exacerbation at <70% of age-predicted maximum heart rate) and typically is associated
with minimal physical examination abnormalities; in addition, symptoms of orthostatic
intolerance and transient oculomotor and vestibular impairments often are present,
which typically resolve spontaneously as the metabolic disturbance subsides.13
Vestibulo-ocular and cervical concussion are not considered to represent an ongoing
global metabolic cerebrovascular disturbance of brain function but are considered
posttraumatic disorders caused by damage to isolated systems. Symptoms are
hypothesized to emanate from injuries to the central oculomotor and vestibular
neurologic subsystems of the brain and/or to the upper cervical spine.13 Patients may
demonstrate late exercise intolerance during systematic exertion testing (ie, symptom
exacerbation beyond 70% of age-predicted maximum heart rate) because of head and
neck motion.14
Mood/cognition-related concussion that manifests soon after injury may be the result of
metabolic disturbance of concussive head injury and typically resolve as the concussed

brain heals. These patients have persistent anxiety, irritability, and/or depressive
symptoms and often experience decreased concentration and short-term recall that
affects school or work performance. Other conditions associated with persistent mood
or cognitive symptoms include vestibular and/or oculomotor problems, aggravation of
preexisting affective states (anxiety, depression), sleep-wake cycle disruption, nocebo
effects of the diagnosis, and posttraumatic pain (eg, headache, cervicalgia); these should
be ruled out.1
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Assessment of concussion in an outpatient clinic is different from that on the sideline. The
examiner should determine the following:
Patient history and mechanism of injury
Immediate symptoms and details on initial medical evaluation and management (eg, loss of
consciousness, transport to emergency department, imaging studies).
Cognitive and emotional symptoms; clinicians can consider using one of the following:
Patient Health Questionnaire-9
Beck Depression Inventory and/or Beck Anxiety Inventory
Medical history—Concussion-induced exacerbation of the following preexisting medical
conditions is strongly associated with delayed recovery (ie, more than 2 weeks in adults and
more than 4 weeks in children/adolescents):
History of three or more concussions
Prior concussion in which symptoms lasted for more than 1 month
Personal or family history of migraine headaches
Learning disorders (eg, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder)
Depression, anxiety, or other mood disorder
Preexisting ophthalmologic conditions, such as strabismus or convergence insufficiency
Patient expectations for recovery


To assess for possible amnesia (either retrograde or anterograde), the clinician should
ask the patient to recall the circumstances of the injury. An observer who can validate
the patient’s story or, if available, video confirmation may be helpful. The clinician should
assess current ongoing symptoms via a validated concussion symptom questionnaire,
such as the Post-Concussion Symptom Inventory for children and teenagers or Post-
Concussion Symptom Scale (22-item list of symptoms scored on a Likert scale from 1 to
6) for adults (Table 1). The symptom load at the initial visit is strongly associated with
duration of recovery; however, symptoms of concussion are not specific and may be
linked to several other disorders. Therefore, each symptom should be assessed for other
possible causes (such as current life stressors or mood problems).14 The Standardized
Assessment of Concussion from the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 5 is the most
common sideline assessment of orientation, memory, and concentration.1 However, the
utility of this questionnaire diminishes substantially 3 to 5 days postinjury and is not
recommended for clinic use.

Physical Examination
The goal of the outpatient clinic assessment is to identify underlying symptom generators to
direct specific management.15
A comprehensive physical examination is warranted because some abnormalities that were
not present on the sideline or in the emergency department may occur 24 to 48 hours
postinjury.1,2
The face, head, pericranial musculature, temporomandibular joints, muscles of mastication,
craniocervical junction, cervical and thoracic spines, and shoulders should be palpated to
screen for associated injuries.
An elemental neurologic assessment (cranial nerves, reflexes, and fundoscopy) should be
performed during the initial assessment if no brain imaging studies have been performed. Any
abnormalities, such as a focal neurologic sign, warrant further investigation.
The concussion-focused physical examination should include the following subsystems:
autonomic, cervical, oculomotor, and vestibular.6


Physical Examination
The clinician can assess the autonomic subsystem via determination of orthostatic
intolerance using the 2-minute supine to 1-minute standing orthostatic hypotension
test.16 A positive result is defined as a complaint of lightheadedness or worsening
dizziness (sensation of motion or vertigo) when assuming the standing position (sitting is
not required). Typically, patients do not meet vital sign criteria for orthostatic
hypotension (ie, drop of ≥20 mm Hg in systolic blood pressure or ≥10 mm Hg in diastolic
blood pressure). Lightheadedness is suggestive of cardiac autonomic dysfunction,
whereas vertigo is suggestive of vestibular dysfunction. Dizziness in the supine position
suggests peripheral vestibular dysfunction, and the clinician should consider additional
tests, such as the Dix-Hallpike maneuver or the cervical joint reposition maneuver.17
Clinicians can evaluate cervical or neck injuries via range of motion and manual
palpation of the neck, suboccipital region, and shoulders. Cervical injuries are commonly
associated with concussion;10 however, they are clinically distinct from the global
metabolic dysfunction of cerebral concussion. Unmanaged cervical impairments are a
frequent cause of PPCS.18, 19
Ocular and vestibular subsystems usually are assessed simultaneously. The Vestibular
Ocular Motor Screening20 assessment is a validated screening protocol for oculomotor
and vestibular impairments after concussion that includes the following tests: repetitive
saccades, smooth pursuits, vestibulo-ocular reflex, visual motion sensitivity, and near
point of convergence. The Balance Error Scoring System and the modified Balance Error
Scoring System are validated tests typically used on the sport sideline.21,22 These tests
also can be used in the office setting to track recovery; however, results tend to return to
baseline values within 4 to 5 days postinjury. Tandem gait—five steps forward and five
steps backward with eyes open and eyes closed—is validated for outpatient use after
concussion to assess dynamic balance. Errors are defined as stepping off the line, raising
the arms, or substantial sway. The total number of errors over the four conditions are
calculated (≤4 errors is normal, whereas ≥5 total errors are abnormal). Tandem gait
forward with eyes open is associated with a high specificity (99%), whereas tandem gait

Additional Testing
Additional tests, including systematic exertion tolerance testing and neurocognitive
assessments, may be warranted in some patients.6
Referral to a neuropsychologist for in-depth cognitive testing is not warranted in most patients
but should be considered if:
Substantial cognition/mood-related dysfunction is observed at the initial visit
Symptoms persist for more than 2 months
The patient requests such a referral

11/23


Additional Testing
Exercise intolerance because of exacerbation of concussion-like symptoms is considered
pathognomonic of physiologic-autonomic dysfunction after concussion.24 Clinicians can
assess exercise tolerance via clinically validated and safe systematic exercise protocols
(eg, the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test or the Buffalo Concussion Bike Test).25
Exercise tolerance testing can be used to aid in diagnosis, design a tailored sub-symptom
threshold aerobic exercise program to speed recovery from a sports-related concussion
(SRC), help manage PPCS, and determine physiologic recovery from concussion and
readiness to return to play (RTP). Computerized neurocognitive tests (eg, Immediate
Post-Concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing)26 are more readily available than a
formal assessment by a neuropsychologist and are most useful if the results are
compared with preinjury test results. However, these tests are limited by concerns
regarding retest reliability and ease of manipulating results based on patient effort.1
Imaging Studies
Advanced imaging studies typically are not useful for the evaluation of concussion, which
remains a clinical diagnosis; by definition, no traumatic abnormality is observed on standard
neuroimaging studies (CT and structural MRI).1
If the clinician is concerned about intracranial bleeding, urgent CT of the head is warranted.
In patients with atypical signs or symptoms and in patients with prolonged recovery who are
not responding to evidence-based treatment, MRI of the brain may be indicated to rule out
occult structural abnormalities.
Differential Diagnosis
Cervical injury (eg, strain or whiplash-associated disorder)—Isolated cervical injury is the most
common mimic of concussion. Patients may present with cervicogenic headache; worsening of
concussion-like symptoms during exercise (because of motion of the head and neck); cognitive
symptoms, such as reduced concentration and short-term recall; and balance problems.
Isolated ocular/oculomotor or vestibular injuries

Anxiety and/or depressive disorders, especially in patients with these preinjury affective
conditions
Inner ear trauma
Posttraumatic migraine headache
Intracranial hemorrhage
Malingering
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
The patient should be removed from sport and other high-risk environments that risk
repeated trauma until clinical clearance.
No pharmacologic or nutraceutical therapies with sufficient empirical evidence to speed
concussion recovery are available; however, some over-the-counter medications may be
useful in symptom management..

Indications
Patients should relatively rest for 24 to 48 hours postinjury (including avoiding school if
attendance may result in worsening symptoms). After symptoms stabilize, patients can
gradually return to daily activities but remain below their individual cognitive and
physical symptom exacerbation thresholds. No scientific evidence shows that strict rest
beyond the first 48 hours is beneficial to recovery. Students should return to school full
time or part time, with appropriate accommodations, as soon as symptoms have
stabilized.27
Academic or work accommodations (eg, limits on computer use, elimination of test
taking) should be considered for patients who report difficulty keeping up at school or
with job requirements. Psychostimulants, such as methylphenidate and amphetamines,
have proven efficacy in patients with more severe forms of traumatic brain injury.28 They
typically are not necessary after concussion; however, clinicians can consider them for

13/23

patients with persistent cognitive fatigue that does not respond to treatment for a mood
or sleep disturbance. Psychostimulants are not indicated for college or professional
athletes because of issues regarding performance-enhancing drugs.
For sleep difficulties, nonpharmacologic behavioral interventions, including sleep
hygiene education and evidence-based cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia,29
should be used initially. Over-the-counter medication, such as melatonin, also may be
useful. Some patients may require a prescription medication and may respond to low-
dose amitriptyline or trazodone.30 Medications such as zolpidem or benzodiazepines
may be indicated in patients with severe sleep deprivation; however, they should be
used only for a short period.31 Persistent insomnia interfering with recovery requires
consultation with a sleep medicine specialist for a formal sleep study and management.
According to the International Concussion in Sport Group consensus statement, mood-
related PPCS is the most challenging concussion subtype to treat.1 Typically,
multidisciplinary management that includes a neuropsychologist; a psychiatrist; and,
perhaps, an occupational therapist is required. Substantial mood symptoms should be
managed in the same manner that mood disorders without concussion are managed,
with evidence-based pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic therapies.
Post-concussion headaches are associated with several potential causes, each of which
requires different management. These headaches include cervicogenic headache,
vestibular and oculomotor-induced headache, tension headache, posttraumatic
migraine, mood-related headache, and exercise-induced headache.32 Preinjury factors
associated with a higher incidence of posttraumatic headache include female sex,
family/personal history of migraine and mood disorders, multiple previous concussions,
and weaker neck strength.18, 19 Management is based on a patient’s history and physical
examination findings, with nonpharmacologic therapies, including cervical physical
therapy, subthreshold aerobic exercise, vestibular rehabilitation, sleep restoration,
vision therapy, and/or cognitive therapy, considered initially. Acetaminophen or NSAIDs
may be used to manage headache (narcotics should be avoided), with medication breaks
taken during the week to avoid the specter of rebound or medication-overuse
headache.33

Outcomes
Most concussion symptoms resolve within a few days to a few weeks, and do not require
intensive medical management. After the first few days of relative rest, patients should be
encouraged to engage in cognitive and low-risk physical activities, with rest breaks as
necessary to avoid exacerbation of concussion symptoms.
Patients with persistent posttraumatic migraine headaches should be referred to a neurologist
or headache specialist.
Complications
A second head injury that occurs while the brain has not recovered from a concussion results
in considerable worsening of symptoms and delays recovery. This scenario is termed
overlapping concussion syndrome.34
Postmortem autopsies in retired contact-sport athletes have identified a distinct tau
proteinopathy, termed chronic traumatic encephalopathy, that is linked to early-onset
dementia (termed traumatic encephalopathy syndrome).35

Complications
Second impact syndrome is a rare but devastating condition reported mostly in male
adolescents injured in contact/collision sport. Second impact syndrome is hypothesized
to occur if a second head injury that occurs before resolution of a first head injury leads
to diffuse axonal injury and uncontrolled cerebral edema. Second impact syndrome is
associated with a high degree of mortality or permanent disability.36
Most of the research on living, retired contact sport athletes, however, shows that the
risk of developing mood and cognitive symptoms of chronic traumatic encephalopathy is
low and may not be the result of concussive head injuries but because of a repetitive
subconcussive hit.35 Prospective, controlled trials are necessary to determine the

15/23

incidence, prevalence, and specific risk factors for chronic traumatic encephalopathy in
living athletes.37
Rehabilitation
The management of concussion has changed drastically in recent years.
The previous standard of care, which was based on animal studies and expert consensus, was
strict physical and cognitive rest until all symptoms resolved. However, such management is
associated with prolonged recovery times and persistent impairments. An early, active
approach to management is recommended.38

Rehabilitation
Recent studies, including randomized controlled trials, show that early, controlled
physical activity safely speeds recovery and may help prevent the development of PPCS
in adolescents after SRC.39 Cervical dysfunction may be managed as soon as it is
identified to improve outcomes and, potentially, prevent PPCS. Treatment modalities
range from warm compresses and stretches to formal physical therapy, pain
management, and imaging studies if indicated.40 Vestibular and ocular/oculomotor
impairments are present in as many as 70% of patients after concussion.20 Most of
these impairments resolve spontaneously without specialized management. If signs
and/or symptoms persist for more than 3 to 4 weeks, referral to a vestibular physical
therapist and/or an occupational therapist (specializing in vision therapy) is indicated.40
Dynamic vestibular examinations or therapy (if required) should be delayed in patients
with substantial cervical dysfunction.
Sub-symptom threshold aerobic exercise has been reported to safely speed recovery in
adolescents after SRC.39 It can be prescribed as early as 48 hours postinjury given that
symptoms at rest are not increasing. Clinicians can refer patients to a physical therapist
or an athletic trainer to determine the heart rate at symptom exacerbation on a systemic
exertion test, such as the Buffalo Concussion Treadmill Test.41 The patient is prescribed
daily aerobic exercise at 80% to 90% of the heart rate threshold on the exertion test. The

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000042
16/23

patient should attempt to exercise for 20 minutes or until symptoms become
exacerbated compared with the pre-exercise resting symptom level. Alternatively,
clinicians can advise patients to perform self-limited aerobic exercise and instruct them
not to exceed their symptom-exacerbation threshold.42
Outcomes
Recovery from SRC typically occurs spontaneously within 2 weeks in adults and within 1 month
in children and adolescents.1
The recovery period for non–sport-related mild traumatic brain injury typically is longer (as
many as 3 months).43
PPCS occurs in approximately 15% to 30% of patients, requiring specific forms of
rehabilitation.
Patients are considered recovered if symptoms have returned to a baseline level at rest and
exertion and physical examination findings are normal.
An evidence-based definition of recovery from concussion is important given the risk of
delayed recovery should repeated injury occur before resolution of the first concussion.
Patients are considered to be clinically recovered if they meet the following criteria1:
1. Symptoms return to a baseline (preinjury) level. Patients may still have some symptoms
that predate the concussion and are associated with a prior medical condition or what
constitute typical life symptoms.
2. Physical examination findings are normal, particularly those that pertain to the vestibular
and oculomotor subsystems.
3. Patients are able to exercise to at least 80% of the age-appropriate maximum heart rate
without symptom exacerbation and/or are able to attend school or work without
concussion-like symptoms or substantial cognitive fatigue.
After being declared recovered by a physician or another appropriate clinician, athletes must
complete a progressive RTP protocol without return of concussion-like symptoms before
returning to full sport participation. Steps in the graduated RTP strategy include the following:
1. Light aerobic exercise (eg, walking, stationary cycling)

AAOS | Concussion and Other Neurologic Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000042
17/23

2. More strenuous aerobic exercise
3. Sport-specific training drills
4. Noncontact drills
5. Full-contact drills
6. Return to full sport participation
If symptoms occur at any step, the patient should resume resting for 24 hours followed by a
return to the previous step. Each step in the progression should last 24 hours; however, the
step may be hastened under expert supervision for athletes and under certain circumstances
(eg, professional level).1
Pearls and Pitfalls
Concussion avoidance is advocated over concussion management. The following guidelines
are associated with a 70% reduction in the concussion incidence rate7:
Use of a properly fitting well-maintained helmet
Policy and rule changes (eg, eliminating body checking in youth ice hockey)
Practice/skill in athletic technique and education about concussions
Additional pearls to improve concussion management include:
Use age-specific guidelines to determine the allowable extent of contact.
Avoid RTP until injuries completely heal.
Educate players, families, and athletic staff to recognize the signs and symptoms of
concussion, and emphasize the importance of honestly reporting potential concussion
symptoms.
